name: Mersiline mesh implant

lead: Mersiline mesh is named in a chin-augmentation reference as a mesh scaffold used to build up the chin or facial area for added projection or volume. The name appears to correspond to Mersilene, a polyester (Dacron) surgical mesh.

Mersilene has been used for decades in hernia repair, prolapse surgery and eyelid-lifting procedures. In looksmaxxing it is a niche hardmaxx implant option. Its facial-augmentation use is mentioned only in passing, and no cosmetic studies were found in the reviewed material.

paras: A woven synthetic mesh is placed as a scaffold within the tissue, the way it is used as reinforcement or suspension material elsewhere in the body. It is listed alongside other alternatives such as acellular dermal matrix and braided suture material.
Cosmetic risks are not documented in the reviewed sources. Studies of Mersilene mesh in other body regions report complications, for example in eyelid ptosis surgery.

chain: Chin or facial area built up
angle.text: A woven polyester mesh is placed as a scaffold to build up the chin or facial area for added projection or volume. A chin-augmentation reference mentions it as an alternative implant material, and the mesh itself is established in hernia and eyelid surgery.

lead: Mersiline mesh is a woven synthetic mesh listed among the materials surgeons can use to build up the chin and other parts of the facial skeleton. In chin augmentation, a mesh scaffold lets surgeons lay a fabric against the bone to add projection or fill a contour, which can make a recessed chin or flat area look stronger in profile. A general reference on chin augmentation names Mersiline alongside acellular dermal matrix and braided suture material (Supramid) as alternatives to the standard silicone, porous polyethylene and ePTFE implants.[1]

The name appears to correspond to Mersilene, an Ethicon polyester (Dacron-type) mesh used for decades in hernia repair, pelvic floor and incontinence surgery, and eyelid-lifting (frontalis suspension) procedures.[2][3][4][5] A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis of alloplastic facial implants included mersilene mesh as one of the materials examined and reported its outcomes alongside those of other implant types.[6]

In looksmaxxing, mesh implants are mentioned as a hardmaxx option for facial contouring. Published cosmetic data specific to Mersiline mesh is limited to the pooled facial-implant analysis, while most of the clinical literature on Mersilene mesh comes from other surgical fields.[2][6]

paras: A general chin augmentation reference lists Mersiline among non-standard chin implant materials, describing it as a mesh that scaffolds the bone. The standard chin options in the same reference are silicone, porous polyethylene (Medpor) and ePTFE (Gore-Tex), which differ in softness and in whether tissue grows into them.[1] That reference also notes synthetic materials are off-the-shelf and spare the patient a donor site, unlike bone grafts from the ribs or pelvis, which are associated with higher infection rates.[1]

Chin implants are usually placed through an incision under the chin or inside the lower lip. Alternatives described in the same source include sliding genioplasty, in which the chin segment of the jaw is cut and moved, and injectable fillers such as hyaluronic acid or calcium hydroxyapatite.[1]

Mersilene is a polyester mesh. Polyethylene terephthalate, the polymer behind polyester fibres, was patented in 1941 by John Rex Whinfield and James Tennant Dickson of the Calico Printers' Association in Manchester, and was later commercialised under brand names including Terylene (ICI) and Dacron (DuPont).[7] Dacron and Mersilene-type meshes then entered surgery as implantable fabrics.

A 1984 review described Dacron (Mersilene) mesh as having been used by two French surgical teams for about 20 years in groin hernia repair.[2] A 1985 report followed 56 patients who underwent abdominal sacral colpopexy for vaginal vault prolapse, in most of whom synthetic mesh was the interposed material.[3]

A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery pooled 17 studies of alloplastic facial implants (2,100 patients, follow-up from one month to 27 years) and stratified outcomes by facial region and material. It reported that mersilene mesh implants carried the highest infection risk among the materials examined (3.38 percent), methyl methacrylate the highest hematoma rate (5.98 percent), and implants in the periorbital region the highest rates of inflammation, explantation and poor cosmetic outcome.[6]

Other research on Mersilene mesh concerns non-cosmetic areas. A retrospective series of 32 eyelids in 20 patients who had Mersilene frontalis sling surgery for ptosis reported good long-term function in about three-quarters of eyelids, with early soft tissue complications in up to 20 percent of patients, and the authors suggested other materials such as monofilament suture or fascia lata could be considered.[4] A case report series described extrusion in two and granuloma formation in three of 79 eyelids (52 patients) operated on with a Mersilene sling.[8] A registered trial compared Proline mesh with Mersilene tape in sacro-hysteropexy for apical prolapse (completed, n=80).[9] A review of alloplastic materials in rhinoplasty is the closest nose-surgery reference.[10]

Reviews and trials from other fields describe the material's broader record. A Cochrane review of materials for frontalis sling surgery in congenital ptosis states that the optimal material is unknown. [11] Clinical studies have examined the Mersilene mesh suburethral sling in women with stress incontinence, including a long-term study of 200 women with complicated forms who were monitored yearly. [12][13] Randomized trials have also compared Mersilene mesh with autogenous fascia lata for congenital blepharoptosis and with sclera for wrapping hydroxyapatite orbital implants. [14][15] No published trial has tested Mersilene mesh specifically as a chin or cheek implant.

Reported complications of Mersilene mesh in other surgical sites include infection, mesh exposure, extrusion and granuloma formation caused by a foreign-body reaction.[4][8] The facial-implant meta-analysis found infection to be the main differentiator for mersilene mesh compared with other materials.[6] For chin implants in general, Wikipedia lists swelling, hematoma and temporary lip numbness as common and minor, and infection, implant displacement and nerve damage as less common.[1]

Mersiline appears in lists of hardmaxx implant options, typically as one of several materials a surgeon might use for chin or facial contouring. Looksmaxxing discussions generally focus on projection and profile, and surgeons' choices among silicone, porous polyethylene, ePTFE, mesh or bone-moving procedures depend on the case.[1]
